lines.text: An agent framework is not a chatbot wrapper; it is a managed, repeatable task runtime.
Google Agent Development Kit is an open-source framework for building, debugging, and deploying production agents.
ADK is available in Python, TypeScript, Go, Java, and Kotlin.
The homepage positioning is explicit: build production agents, not prototypes.
You can start with a prompt and tools, then grow into multi-agent orchestration and graph workflows.
ADK is designed to be written by both humans and AI coding assistants.
The kit works with Gemini and many other models, including hosted and local options.
Context is treated like source code: sessions, memory, tools, and artifacts are assembled, not pasted until overflow.
The fundamental worker is an Agent, usually an LlmAgent for reasoning, or a workflow agent for deterministic control.
A Tool gives the agent abilities beyond conversation: APIs, search, code, and other services.
Callbacks run at defined points so you can inspect, log, or change behavior without rewriting the agent core.
A Session holds one conversation thread: events, history, and working State.
Memory is long-term knowledge across sessions, distinct from short-term session State.
Artifacts let agents save and load files or binary data associated with a session or user.
An Event is the unit of communication: user message, agent reply, or tool use.
The Runner is the engine that orchestrates execution from events and coordinates backend services.
Python ADK requires Python 3.10 or later, then pip install google-adk.
adk create scaffolds a project with agent.py, a dotenv file, and package init.
The only required element is a root_agent definition in agent.py.
A first agent can be a Gemini model, an instruction, and one Python function used as a tool.
Gemini API use needs GOOGLE_API_KEY in the environment, never committed to source control.
adk run starts an interactive command-line session against your agent folder.
adk web starts a local chat UI, typically on port 8000, launched from the parent folder.
The documentation warns that ADK Web is for development and debugging, not production deployments.
A tool is developer-defined logic. It does not reason on its own; the model chooses when to call it.
The loop is reason, select, invoke with arguments, then fold the result back into the next step.
Function tools wrap ordinary functions. Clear names and docstrings drive tool selection.
You can also wrap another agent as AgentTool, or connect MCP and OpenAPI surfaces.
Long-running tools exist for asynchronous work that should not block the whole turn.
Action confirmations let you gate dangerous tool calls before they execute.
Agent Skills package instructions, resources, and tools, loaded on demand to protect the context window.
The Skills feature is experimental; treat it as evolving, not as a frozen contract.
A workflow begins when more than one agent or executable node must cooperate.
Split when instructions get unreliable, context overflows, or you need reusable modules.
Template workflow agents are Sequential, Parallel, and Loop. They orchestrate without asking a model how to route.
ADK 2.0 adds graph-based workflows: nodes and edges with explicit routing for deterministic control.
Dynamic workflows use your own code for loops, branching, and recursion that a static graph cannot express cleanly.
Collaborative workflows use coordinator agents and sub-agents working together.
Python ADK 2.0 reached general availability on 19 May 2026.
Agents, tools, and functions become nodes in the workflow graph; review breaking changes before you upgrade 1.x apps.
Context is the bundle of state, artifacts, memory, and credentials available during one invocation.
The framework creates InvocationContext. You rarely construct it by hand.
Session history and State cover the current thread only, such as a cart in this chat.
Memory is a searchable archive across past sessions or external knowledge.
Memory services can ingest a session, append a delta, add facts, and search. Not every backend implements every method.
In-memory session and memory implementations are for local testing, not production durability.
ADK can filter irrelevant events, summarize older turns, lazy-load artifacts, and track token use.
Treat context like source code: every token should earn its place.
Development runtimes include the CLI, the web UI, an API server, and ambient event-driven agents.
The event loop is a yield, pause, and resume cycle, not a single blocking script.
You can resume and cancel runs; design long jobs so interruption is recoverable.
Deploy to Agent Runtime for a managed agent service, Cloud Run for containers, or GKE for Kubernetes control.
You can also containerize and run anywhere Docker or Podman can run, including offline hosts.
Agent evaluation scores both the final answer and the trajectory of tool steps.
Compare expected steps such as determine intent, use tool, review results, then generate the report.
If you intend to leave the prototype stage, automated evaluation is a documented best practice, not optional polish.
Uncontrolled agents can take misaligned actions, including data exfiltration.
Control identity: decide whether the agent acts as itself or as the user.
Use input and output guardrails, in-tool policies, callbacks, plugins, and Gemini content filters.
Sandbox model-generated code, and confine cloud activity with network controls such as VPC Service Controls.
Local sub-agents organize code in-process. Remote A2A agents are separate services on a network.
Use A2A when languages, teams, or standalone services must share a formal agent contract.
Do not use ADK Web in production. Authenticate to Google Cloud with ADC or a service account, never committed keys.
Start with one LlmAgent and one tool, measure the trajectory, then add graphs, memory, and deployment from evidence.
